Stopping between segments

Accelerating on the final 1kms
Recovery too short

descriptionEn: Ladder session: 3km at half-marathon pace, 2x1km at target 10K pace, 2x1km at 5K pace. 3min recovery between sets. Develops ability to accelerate on tired legs.

Mentally demanding session
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast on the half-marathon 3km
Not accelerating enough on the 5K portion
Cutting the recovery times

descriptionEn: Mixed half/10K session: 1km at half pace, 4km at target 10K pace, 2x2km at half pace. 2min recovery between sets. Works on pace alternation.

The 4km 10K block is the heart of the session
Finishing at half pace = return to control
Excellent for half-marathon preparation

Not dropping back to half pace afterwards
Recovery too short between blocks

descriptionEn: 6km block at target 10K pace. Confidence session to do 10 days before the race. Validates ability to hold pace for more than half the target distance.

Builds confidence for race day
If you can hold 6km, you can hold 10km
Don't push too hard, just validate the pace
Session that boosts mental confidence
commonMistakesEn: Running faster than target pace
Doing this session too close to the race
Not benefiting from the confidence effect

coachingTipsEn: Reproduce your exact race routine
Note the timings for race day
Test your outfit and shoes
Finish 5-10min before fictional start
Memorize the feeling of being ready

Forgetting part of the routine
Getting tired with too many accelerations

descriptionEn: Introduction to 5K pace. Three short repetitions to get familiar with race-specific intensity without overloading.

The 3min recovery allows full recovery between efforts
Focus on maintaining a steady rhythm
Ideal session for discovering your specific speed
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast on the first repetition
Confusing 5K pace with sprinting
Not respecting the recovery time

descriptionEn: Gentle introduction to 10K-specific pace. Three 5-minute blocks to accustom the body to sustained effort.
coachingTipsEn: 10K pace = approximately 85-90% HRmax
Sustained effort but not maximal
The 3min recovery allows a good cooldown between efforts
First step before longer 10K-specific sessions
commonMistakesEn: Running at 5K pace instead of 10K
Starting too fast and not holding the 5 minutes
Walking during recovery instead of jogging

descriptionEn: Progressive introduction to half-marathon pace. Two 10-minute blocks to learn managing a prolonged effort.
coachingTipsEn: Half-marathon pace = controlled effort, regular breathing
You should be able to say a few words between breaths
The 5min recovery is important: don't shorten it
Stepping-stone session toward race-pace long runs
commonMistakesEn: Running the first block too fast
Confusing half-marathon pace with 10K pace
Not warming up enough before the effort

descriptionEn: First steps at marathon pace. Two 12-minute blocks to learn the marathon cruising rhythm.
coachingTipsEn: Marathon pace = comfortable but sustained
You should be able to hold a conversation in short sentences
Memorize this feeling: it's your cruising speed
Foundation session for marathon preparation
commonMistakesEn: Running too fast, at half-marathon pace instead of marathon
Not using a GPS watch to calibrate pace
Shortening the recovery between blocks

descriptionEn: Target race distance (e.g. 10K) run at race pace, split into 3 equal segments with 3-4 minutes jog recovery between each segment. Allows practicing specific pace over the full distance with less stress than a time trial.

steps.description: 3,3 km à allure 10K (ou 3 × 7 km à allure semi)
steps.descriptionEn: 3.3km at 10K pace (or 3 × 7km at half-marathon pace), 3-4min jog recovery between each segment

mainSetTemplate.description: 3 × 3,3 km à allure 10K (ou 3 × 7 km à allure semi), récup 3-4min trot entre chaque segment
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 3 × 3.3km at 10K pace (or 3 × 7km at half-marathon pace), 3-4min jog recovery between each segment

coachingTipsEn: The pace of each segment must match exactly your target race pace
Short recoveries allow maintaining quality over the total distance
Adapt the distance to your goal: 10K as 3×3.3km, half as 3×7km, 5K as 3×1.7km
Ideal 2-3 weeks before the target race as a lower-stress dress rehearsal

Taking too much recovery (>5 minutes) between segments
Scheduling this session too far from competition for it to have specific impact

descriptionEn: 4 repetitions of 5km at marathon pace (100-103%) with 1km 'recovery' at 85-90% of marathon pace between each. Total quality volume: approximately 24km. Develops fatigue resistance at marathon-specific pace with insufficient recovery.

mainSetTemplate.description: 4 × 5 km à 100-103% allure marathon (Z3), avec 1 km récup à 85-90% allure marathon entre chaque (jamais en dessous de Z2 haut)
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 4 × 5km at 100-103% marathon pace (Z3), with 1km 'recovery' at 85-90% marathon pace between each (never below upper Z2)

coachingTipsEn: Recovery kilometers stay at 85-90% marathon pace, this is not easy jogging
Total volume (~30km including warm-up and cool-down) makes this a key marathon preparation session
Schedule this session 6-10 weeks before the marathon, followed by 5-7 easy days
If you cannot maintain pace on the 4th block, the session is too ambitious: reduce to 3 × 5km
commonMistakesEn: Turning recovery kilometers into easy jogging instead of staying at 85-90% marathon pace
Running the 5km blocks too fast (above 103% marathon pace) at the start of the session
Scheduling this session without planning sufficient recovery in the following days

descriptionEn: Very slow jog in Zone 1 to promote active recovery. Easy conversational pace, nasal breathing should be possible.

If you can't breathe through your nose, slow down
Choose flat and soft terrain
commonMistakesEn: Running too fast - this is the easiest session of the week
Skipping this session when it's crucial for recovery

descriptionEn: Alternating brisk walking and very light jogging. Ideal for beginners or after a race/competition.

Hydrate well before and after

Alternate front / back if possible to balance

Head out of the water on the board, breaks alignment

Letting technique slip under the guise of fatigue

coachingTipsEn: Strong hiking on climbs taxes the aerobic system as much as jogging; it is not rest
Carry water and a snack beyond 75 minutes, even on an easy outing
This session replaces the road long run during a trail build-up
Log elevation rather than distance: elevation is what measures trail load
commonMistakesEn: Running every climb at all costs and finishing the outing empty
Neglecting the descents, which are the leading source of trail soreness
Picking a route with too much elevation for a first long outing

coachingTipsEn: Hands on thighs, torso forward, short fast steps: ultra hiking is a push, not a stroll
Chase cadence, not stride length, 50 to 60 steps per minute per leg on a steep gradient
With poles, plant them ahead of the foot and push through the end of the stroke: they carry 10 to 15% of the effort
Time the same segment hiked and run: above 15% gradient, hiking almost always wins
commonMistakesEn: Hiking with arms dangling, which leaves every bit of the work to the legs
Running the climb out of principle and cresting ten beats too high for what follows
Discovering poles on race day, where they get in the way more than they help

coachingTipsEn: Two light sources, always: a headlamp and a backup, with fresh batteries checked before you leave
A headlamp worn low flattens the terrain; adding a waist lamp draws the rocks out by their shadows
Tell someone where you are going and when you will be back. That is the one non-negotiable rule of this session
Take one more layer than in daytime: your pace drops and your temperature follows
commonMistakesEn: Discovering your headlamp on race night and finding it lights descents badly
Using daytime pace for your night splits and building an impossible race plan
Heading out alone on a technical trail you have never seen in daylight

coachingTipsEn: Write everything down: what went in, at what time, and what came back up. It is the only way to own a fuelling plan rather than an intention
Build up gradually: 60g of carbohydrate an hour first, 90g only once 60 passes without complaint
Drink what the race will serve, an unknown organiser's drink at kilometre 40 is a gamble
Alternate solid and liquid: three hours of gels alone rarely ends well
commonMistakesEn: Eating nothing in training and everything in the race, hoping it holds
Trying the top quantities on the first outing and spending the afternoon doubled over
Counting only carbohydrate and forgetting sodium, which decides what actually gets absorbed

coachingTipsEn: The cue is not the clock but your breathing: you should manage a short sentence, not a conversation
Same gradient for all four reps: a different gradient makes it a different session and the comparison worthless
The descent is recovery, not technical work: jog it, do not train eccentric load here
Twice a week at most during a build, and never the day before a long run

Picking too steep a gradient, which turns the session into disguised power hiking

Volume goes up without any single run becoming crushing, and the second one is run on legs that have already worked, a back-to-back in miniature, absorbed in two days instead of ten.
